Psychological continuity alone does not account for all aspects of personal identity. For example, there are cases where a person can experience themselves as the same person despite changes in their psychological states or experiences, such as cases of severe neurological damage or haxamnesia. These cases suggest that identity may be partly or completely independent of psychological continuity.

Consider the case of a person who has had their memories wiped clean through amnesia but is able to form new memories and experience themselves as the same person over time. This suggests that their self-concept and sense of identity are not solely based on psychological continuity.

One could argue that psychological continuity is not the only necessary condition for personal identity. For instance, a person could have a consistent self over time without experiencing psychological continuity, such as in the case of a person who has amnesia but maintains a consistent identity through social interactions and memories shared with others.
